title: Short forms (present)
titleJp: あした 何 する？
canDo: I can turn any verb from the ます form into the dictionary form and the ない form (食べます → 食べる → 食べない), including the special cases かう → かわない and ある → ない.
I can say the short form of い-adjectives, な-adjectives and nouns, affirmative and negative (高い / 高くない; しずかだ / しずかじゃない; 学生だ / 学生じゃない).
I can chat with a friend in casual style: ask without か and without だ (ひま？) and answer with うん / ううん.
I can recognize a casual line (in a game, in an anime) and say what the polite version with です / ます would be.

blocks.t: Warm-up: say the ます form of 10 verbs from Genki Lessons 3–7 out loud (食べます, 飲みます, 行きます…)
Vocabulary: tap 🔊 on each word and repeat it twice
Grammar: the 3 points, each with its examples read aloud and one 🔬
Block 6: the Lesson 8 video (pause on the conjugation tables) or the Sakubi sections, read once to understand, not to memorize
Notebook homework + checking it against the answer key
Checklist (block 10) + write your questions in the lesson notebook

skills: Knowing the ます form of the verbs from Genki Lessons 3–7 and which group each one belongs to: る-verb, う-verb or irregular (lessons 03-1 and 06-1).
Conjugating い- and な-adjectives in the polite present, affirmative and negative: 高いです / 高くないです; しずかです / しずかじゃないです (lesson 05-1).
Reading the Genki Lesson 3–8 kanji used in the examples (食, 飲, 行, 休, 仕事, 会社員…). The kana reading is always shown next to them.

vocab.en: to rest; to take a day off, to be absent (from work, class) · う-verb
to go back, to return (home) · う-verb, even though it ends in -eru
there is; to have (things) · negative: ない

grammar.title: Verbs: dictionary form and ない
grammar.explanation:
So far you have said everything in the **polite** style, with です and ます. Every verb also has a **short form** (Genki's name for it; other guides say "plain form"), which says the same thing without the layer of politeness. It has two jobs: **talking with friends and family** (point 4c) and **building new grammar**. In lesson 08-2, for example, 〜と 思います only works with the short form.
• **Affirmative = dictionary form**, the form dictionaries list: 食べます → **食べる**, 飲みます → **飲む**, します → **する**. In う-verbs, the sound before ます (-i) becomes -u: のみます → のむ, まちます → まつ, かいます → かう. Like the ます form, it covers the present **and the future**: 休む = "I rest" or "I'll rest".
• **Why two groups?** A **る-verb** has **one** fixed base that never changes: たべ + る / ない / ます. An **う-verb** keeps its base but **moves its last vowel** across the five vowels: のま-ない, のみ-ます, のむ (the other two come later). That is why Sakubi calls them "one-form" and "five-form" verbs.
• **Telling them apart**: a verb ending in any sound other than る (う, く, す, つ, む…) is always an う-verb. A る-verb always ends in -iru or -eru (みる, たべる), but a few -iru / -eru verbs are う-verbs (かえる, はいる). Learn the group together with the word.
• **Negative = ない form**, which replaces ません.
• **る-verbs**: drop る and add ない: たべる → たべない, みる → みない.
• **う-verbs**: change the final -u to -a and add ない: のむ → のまない, かく → かかない, はなす → はなさない, まつ → またない, かえる → かえらない.
• **Verbs ending in う**: the -a becomes **わ**, not あ: かう → かわない, あう → あわない, いう → いわない.
• **Irregulars**: Japanese has only two, and both are very common: する → しない, くる → **こない** (く becomes こ).
• **ある → ない**: the negative of ある is just ない.
The block's job does not change: the verb is still the **predicate**, at the end of the sentence. Only the register becomes informal.
• Going further (Sakubi): the ない at the end is itself an い-adjective, so it conjugates like one. The past of 飲まない will be 飲まなかった, just like 高くない → 高くなかった (lesson 09-1).
grammar.structure: [る-verb] たべる → たべない · [う-verb] のむ → のまない (-u → -a + ない) · する → しない · くる → こない · ある → ない

examples.jp: 今日は 仕事を 休む。
examples.kana: きょうは しごとを やすむ。
examples.en: I'm taking the day off work today.

examples.jp: ペドロは おさけを 飲まない。
examples.kana: ペドロは おさけを のまない。

examples.jp: 今 お金が ない。
examples.kana: いま おかねが ない。
examples.en: I don't have any money right now. [lit. now, money doesn't exist]

pitfalls: Verbs ending in う take わ in the negative: かう → かわない ✓, かあない ✗. The same goes for あう, いう, あらう.
The negative of ある is ない ✓, not あらない ✗. いる (people, animals), on the other hand, is regular: いない ✓.
かえる and はいる look like る-verbs, but they are う-verbs: かえらない ✓ (かえない ✗), はいらない ✓ (はいない ✗). That's why it pays to learn each verb's group together with the word.
The two irregulars: くる becomes こない ✓, not くない ✗; する becomes しない ✓, not すない ✗.
howToStudy: Take 10 verbs from Genki Lessons 3–7 and say the three forms out loud: ます → dictionary → ない (飲みます → 飲む → 飲まない). In your notebook, sort them into three columns: る, う and irregular.

In ヅオリンゴー, do Drills → Conjugation with the verbs you already know, paying attention to the ones ending in う (かう, あう, いう). Then take 2 verbs from a Wagotabi line and look them up in a dictionary (Jisho, in the Resources tab): dictionaries list verbs under the dictionary form, so this is the form you will search with from now on.
Tap 🔬 on the Pedro example: 飲まない is still the PREDICATE and おさけを is still the OBJECT. Only the verb form changed.

grammar.title: Adjectives and nouns in the short form
grammar.gloss: 高い · しずかだ · 学生だ
grammar.explanation:
Adjectives and nouns have short forms too. The practical rule: **take off です** and look at what is left.
• **い-adjective**: 高いです → **高い**; 高くないです → **高くない**. No だ after the い.
• **な-adjective**: しずかです → **しずかだ**; しずかじゃないです → **しずかじゃない**.
• **Noun**: 学生です → **学生だ**; 学生じゃないです → **学生じゃない**.
• **いい** is still irregular: いい → **よくない**.
**Why only some take だ?** (Sakubi's framing) An **い-adjective acts like a verb**: 高い already means "is expensive" on its own, and the です in 高いです only adds politeness. Take the politeness away and nothing is missing. A **noun or な-adjective acts like a noun**: it has no "is" of its own, so its short form needs **だ**, the short version of です. And じゃない is simply the negative of だ.
Every negative ends in ない, which behaves like an い-adjective, so it never takes だ either.
The block is still the **predicate**: 高い alone at the end is already a complete sentence ("it's expensive").
• Going further (Sakubi): in books, signs and formal writing you will also see **ではない** (学生ではない). It is the full, more formal form; じゃない is its spoken contraction.
grammar.structure: [い-adj] 高い / 高くない · [な-adj] しずかだ / しずかじゃない · [noun] 学生だ / 学生じゃない

examples.jp: 今日は あつくない。
examples.kana: きょうは あつくない。

examples.jp: 私の まちは しずかじゃない。
examples.kana: わたしの まちは しずかじゃない。
examples.romaji: Watashi no machi wa shizuka ja nai.

examples.jp: ルーカスは 学生じゃない。会社員だ。
examples.kana: ルーカスは がくせいじゃない。かいしゃいんだ。
examples.romaji: Rūkasu wa gakusei ja nai. Kaishain da.
examples.en: Lucas isn't a student. He's an office worker.

pitfalls: Don't put だ after an い-adjective: 高いだ ✗ → 高い ✓. It already contains its own "is".
The negative of いい is よくない ✓, not いくない ✗.
きれい and きらい end in い, but they are な-adjectives: きれいじゃない ✓, きれくない ✗.
Don't add だ to ない: 高くないだ ✗ → 高くない ✓. The negative is already complete.
howToStudy: In your notebook, make a 4-column table (polite affirmative / polite negative / short affirmative / short negative) with 3 い-adjectives, 3 な-adjectives and 2 nouns. Include いい → よくない. Circle every だ: they should appear only in the な-adjective and noun rows.
Say 5 short sentences about your town and your home out loud, using only short forms: サンパウロは 大きい。うちは しずかじゃない。…
Tap 🔬 on the Lucas example: these are two sentences, and each one has its own PREDICATE at the end (学生じゃない and 会社員だ).

grammar.title: Casual speech
grammar.explanation:
With friends, family and the people closest to you, Japanese ends sentences with the **short form** instead of です / ます. The content is the same; what changes is the distance between the speakers.
• **Questions**: か usually drops, and the question is carried only by your **voice rising** at the end: 飲む？ ("are you going to drink?").
• **だ disappears in questions**: 学生？ ("are you a student?"), ひま？ ("are you free?"). Don't say 学生だ？.
• **In statements**, だ is correct, but on its own it can sound blunt. In conversation people often answer with just the noun (うん、学生。) or soften it with よ (学生だよ).
• **Yes / no**: はい and いいえ become **うん** and **ううん**.
• **Particles drop**: は and を often disappear in casual speech, and sometimes the destination に does too: カラオケ 行く？ When that happens, work out the block's job **from the verb** at the end.
When in doubt (a teacher, a boss, someone you just met), stay with です / ます. This lesson's culture note explains who you can switch with.
• Going further (Sakubi): casual questions often end in **の**: 行くの？, 食べないの？ With nouns and な-adjectives, だ turns into な: ひまなの？ It sounds softer and asks for an explanation; you will study it with 〜んです (lesson 12-1). You will also hear **ええ**, a gentle "yes", and **いや**, a blunter "no".
grammar.structure: [short form]？ (voice rises) → うん、[short form]。 / ううん、[negative short form]。

examples.jp: しゅうまつ、ひま？— うん、ひま。
examples.kana: しゅうまつ、ひま？— うん、ひま。
examples.en: Free this weekend? — Yeah, I'm free.

examples.jp: こんばん カラオケ 行く？— ううん、行かない。仕事が ある。
examples.kana: こんばん カラオケ いく？— ううん、いかない。しごとが ある。
examples.romaji: Konban karaoke iku? — Uun, ikanai. Shigoto ga aru.
examples.en: Going to karaoke tonight? — No, I'm not going. I have work.

examples.jp: ルーカスの せんこう、れきし？— ううん、れきしじゃない。けいざい。
examples.kana: ルーカスの せんこう、れきし？— ううん、れきしじゃない。けいざい。
examples.romaji: Rūkasu no senkō, rekishi? — Uun, rekishi ja nai. Keizai.
examples.en: Is Lucas's major history? — No, it's not history. It's economics.

pitfalls: Don't use casual speech with a teacher, a boss or an older person you have just met. When in doubt, です / ます ✓.
A casual question with a noun or な-adjective takes no だ: ひま？ ✓, ひまだ？ ✗.
In a casual question, か usually drops: 行く？ ✓. 行くか？ exists, but it tends to sound rough; avoid it for now ✗.

ううん (no) is longer than うん (yes), and its melody is different too: tap 🔊 on both in the vocabulary and copy them. If you are afraid of mixing them up, say the whole sentence: ううん、行かない ✓, not just a bare ううん.
howToStudy: Turn 5 polite questions from this and earlier lessons into casual ones, out loud: 行きますか → 行く？; ひまですか → ひま？; 学生ですか → 学生？
Tap 🔬 on the karaoke example: カラオケ shows up as NO PARTICLE. Ask the verb 行く which particle dropped (に, the destination).
Record a mini-dialogue of 4 lines (two questions and two answers), doing both voices. Listen and check that your voice rises at the end of the questions.

homework.intro: Do it by hand in your notebook. Write the kanji you already know and the rest in kana. Only then open the answer key, item by item. Circle what you got wrong and redo it the next day.

tasks.prompt: Write the dictionary form and the ない form of each verb.

items.note: る-verb: drop る and add ない.
Verb ending in う: the -a becomes わ.
It looks like a る-verb, but it is an う-verb.
The negative of ある is just ない.

tasks.prompt: Change each sentence into the short form, keeping it affirmative or negative.

items.note: い-adjective: just take off です.
きれい is a な-adjective, even though it ends in い.

tasks.prompt: Rewrite each dialogue in casual style, as a conversation between friends.

items.q: 日曜日、ひまですか。— はい、ひまです。

a.jp: 日曜日、ひま？— うん、ひま。
a.kana: にちようび、ひま？— うん、ひま。

items.note: A question without か and without だ; はい becomes うん.

items.q: コーヒーを 飲みますか。— いいえ、飲みません。

a.jp: コーヒー 飲む？— ううん、飲まない。
a.kana: コーヒー のむ？— ううん、のまない。

items.note: In casual speech を usually drops, but コーヒーを 飲む？ is also correct.

items.q: マリアさんは 日本人ですか。— いいえ、日本人じゃないです。ブラジル人です。

a.jp: マリアさん、日本人？— ううん、日本人じゃない。ブラジル人。
a.kana: マリアさん、にほんじん？— ううん、にほんじんじゃない。ブラジルじん。
a.romaji: Maria-san, nihonjin? — Uun, nihonjin ja nai. Burajirujin.

items.note: No だ in the question. In the answer, the bare noun (ブラジル人。) sounds natural. If you are close friends, you can also drop the さん.

items.q: その 本、おもしろいですか。— はい、とても おもしろいです。

a.jp: その 本、おもしろい？— うん、とても おもしろい。
a.kana: その ほん、おもしろい？— うん、とても おもしろい。
a.romaji: Sono hon, omoshiroi? — Un, totemo omoshiroi.

items.note: い-adjective: just take off です. No だ.

items.q: あした 大学に 行きますか。— いいえ、行きません。うちで 休みます。

a.jp: あした 大学 行く？— ううん、行かない。うちで 休む。
a.kana: あした だいがく いく？— ううん、いかない。うちで やすむ。
a.romaji: Ashita daigaku iku? — Uun, ikanai. Uchi de yasumu.

items.note: に can also drop in a casual question; 大学に 行く？ is still correct.

tasks.prompt: Write a casual message of 4–5 sentences to a friend: ask if they are free this weekend and say what you do and don't have to do. Use only short forms. Then read it aloud.

items.q: Model (match its structure, not its words):

a.jp: しゅうまつ、ひま？土曜日は 仕事が ある。でも、日曜日は 仕事が ない。うちで ブラジルりょうりを 作る。いっしょに 食べる？
a.kana: しゅうまつ、ひま？どようびは しごとが ある。でも、にちようびは しごとが ない。うちで ブラジルりょうりを つくる。いっしょに たべる？
a.romaji: Shūmatsu, hima? Doyōbi wa shigoto ga aru. Demo, nichiyōbi wa shigoto ga nai. Uchi de burajiru ryōri o tsukuru. Issho ni taberu?
a.en: Free this weekend? I have work on Saturday. But on Sunday I don't have work. I'm going to make Brazilian food at home. Want to eat together?

items.note: Check: no です / ます anywhere; questions without か and without だ; negatives with ない (ある → ない); no だ after an い-adjective.

workbook.tip: Do it after point 4c; check it with the official Genki Answer Key.

practice.what: Play normally and watch for lines that end without です / ます (a dictionary-form verb, ない, うん / ううん, a question without か). Copy 2 of them into your notebook and write the polite version next to each. Save the clearest one with ヅオリンゴー's Mining (⛏), so it comes back in your reviews.

Practice L8 (short-form conjugation) and Drills → Conjugation. Then the Lesson 8 vocabulary in the SRS: learn the new kanji through their words (仕事, 会社員, 休む, 作る) rather than one by one. Do every review that is due; if they pile up, add fewer new words instead of skipping reviews.
Tap 🔊 on the dialogues in point 4c and repeat along 3 times, with the same intonation: your voice rises at the end of the question, with no か.
Record the homework message (h4) as if it were a voice message to a friend, in 30 seconds or less. Listen and check that no です slipped in.

From this lesson on, try a little real reading: most stories and manga are written in short forms. In the Resources tab, open Tadoku's free graded readers and read one level-0 story for the gist, looking up only the words that block the story. Pick out 3 verbs or adjectives and say both forms out loud, short and polite (行く / 行きます).

culture.title: Seniors and juniors (せんぱい／こうはい)
culture.body: In Japanese schools, clubs and companies, relationships are usually organized by **who joined first**: the senior is the **せんぱい** and whoever came later is the **こうはい**, even if the difference is only one year. In general, the こうはい speaks to the せんぱい in です / ます, and the せんぱい may answer in the short form. Among classmates or people of the same age, casual speech tends to appear quickly. The switch to casual speech usually comes from the person "above", sometimes with a line like タメ口で いいよ ("you can talk to me casually"). Many Japanese people are flexible with foreigners, but starting with です / ます is never a mistake.
culture.try: List 5 people in your life (a boss, a classmate, a sibling, a teacher, a friend) and mark each one せんぱい, こうはい or "same level". Then ask each of them the same question in the right register: しゅうまつ、ひまですか。 or しゅうまつ、ひま？

checklist: I can turn any verb from the ます form into the dictionary form and the ない form without looking.
I get the special cases right: かう → かわない, ある → ない, くる → こない, かえる → かえらない.
I can say the short form of い-adjectives, な-adjectives and nouns, affirmative and negative (and いい → よくない).
I never put だ after an い-adjective or in a casual question.
I can ask and answer casual questions with うん / ううん, with my voice rising on the question.
I know who I can speak casually with and when to stay with です / ます.
I did the homework, checked it against the answer key and redid what I got wrong.
